title: WHY DID LEVITICUS FORBID A MAN FROM MARRYING HIS BROTHER’S WIFE—WHILE DEUTERONOMY SOMETIMES REQUIRED IT?
paragraphs: WHY DID LEVITICUS FORBID A MAN FROM MARRYING HIS BROTHER’S WIFE—WHILE DEUTERONOMY SOMETIMES REQUIRED IT?

One verse calls it forbidden. Another tells a brother to do it. Critics call it a contradiction. But when you read the Hebrew carefully, something far more profound appears—and hidden inside this difficult law is a breathtaking picture of responsibility, redemption, and ultimately the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Imagine opening your Bible and discovering two commands that seem to collide.
Leviticus says:
“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy brother's wife: it is thy brother's nakedness.” — Leviticus 18:16
Clear enough.
Your brother's wife is forbidden to you.
Then you turn several books forward and Moses appears to say almost the opposite.

“If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger: her husband's brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife...” — Deuteronomy 25:5
Wait.
What?
Leviticus says, “Do not.”
Deuteronomy says, under certain circumstances, “Do.”
Did Moses contradict Moses?
Did God's moral standard change somewhere between Leviticus and Deuteronomy?
Or have we missed something because we are reading two sentences while ignoring the circumstances surrounding them?
Stay with this, because the answer is much bigger than an obscure ancient marriage law.

And strangely enough, by the time we reach Jesus, this seemingly uncomfortable question about a widow and her brother-in-law will lead us straight into a conversation about resurrection, covenant faithfulness, and a God who refuses to abandon His people to death.
Start with the Hebrew.
Leviticus 18:16 reads:
עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָחִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה עֶרְוַת אָחִיךָ הִוא
‘Ervat eshet-achikha lo tegalleh; ‘ervat achikha hi.
The essential sense is:
“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother's wife; it is your brother's nakedness.”
The language belongs to the sexual-boundary laws of Leviticus 18.
The point is not mysterious.
A man's marriage creates a boundary his brother is not free to violate.
His brother's wife does not become sexually available merely because they are relatives, attracted to each other, living nearby, unhappy with their circumstances, or able to invent a justification.
She is his brother's wife.
There is a boundary.
Leviticus 20:21 reinforces the seriousness of that boundary:
וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יִקַּח אֶת־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיו נִדָּה הִוא
Ve'ish asher yiqqach et-eshet achiv, niddah hi...
“If a man takes his brother's wife, it is impurity/indecency...”
The ordinary rule is therefore unmistakable: a man does not take his brother's wife.
Then comes Deuteronomy 25.
But notice what has changed.
The brother is dead.
And the text specifies another crucial circumstance: he has died without offspring.
Now read the Hebrew:
כִּי־יֵשְׁבוּ אַחִים יַחְדָּו וּמֵת אַחַד מֵהֶם וּבֵן אֵין־לוֹ...
Ki-yeshevu achim yachdav, umet achad mehem, uven ein-lo...
“When brothers dwell together, and one of them dies and has no offspring...”
Then comes remarkable vocabulary:
יְבָמָהּ יָבֹא עָלֶיהָ וּלְקָחָהּ לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה וְיִבְּמָהּ
Yevamah yavo ‘aleha, uleqachah lo le'ishshah, veyibbemah.
Her husband's brother is to take her as his wife and perform the duty of a husband's brother toward her.
That final Hebrew word matters enormously.
וְיִבְּמָהּ — veyibbemah.
It comes from the same word-family associated with yavam, a husband's brother in this special relationship, and yevamah, the widow in the levirate relationship.
In other words, Deuteronomy is not casually overturning Leviticus.
It is describing a specifically defined covenantal circumstance.
The general boundary remains.
But God Himself legislates a particular exception for a particular tragedy.
The brother has died.
He has left no offspring.
His household faces extinction.
His widow faces a vulnerable future in the social world of ancient Israel.
His name and inheritance are in danger of disappearing from his family line.
And suddenly the surviving brother is no longer looking at another man's wife as an object of desire.
He is looking at his dead brother's widow as someone toward whom covenant responsibility may now be required.
That changes everything.
This is why reading isolated Bible verses can be dangerous.
Leviticus addresses a forbidden union.
Deuteronomy addresses a defined levirate obligation.
Same woman in terms of family relationship.
Radically different covenant circumstance.
One situation would violate the brother's marriage.
The other arises because death has ended that marriage and, in the specified childless situation, Israel's law places a responsibility upon the surviving family.
Deuteronomy then tells us why.
The firstborn resulting from the union was to continue the deceased brother's name so that, as the text says, “his name be not blotted out of Israel.”
Read that slowly.
This wasn't primarily a loophole for male desire.
It carried responsibility.
Legacy.
Family.
Inheritance.
Protection.
Name.
Continuity after death.
The surviving brother was being summoned to shoulder a cost for the sake of someone who could no longer repay him.
And that makes what happened with Onan in Genesis 38 much easier to understand.
Long before Deuteronomy formally codified Israel's levirate legislation, Judah told Onan to fulfill his duty toward Tamar after the death of his brother Er.
But Onan knew the offspring would not be reckoned as his brother's in the ordinary sense of family continuation, and he deliberately frustrated that responsibility.
His sin was not merely some isolated biological act ripped from its narrative.
The text emphasizes that he refused the responsibility attached to preserving his brother's line.
He wanted the sexual access while rejecting the costly obligation.
And suddenly an ancient story begins sounding painfully modern.
We want benefits without covenant.
Pleasure without responsibility.
Grace without repentance.
Christianity without surrender.
A Savior without a Lord.
Heaven without holiness.
Forgiveness without admitting there is anything from which we need to be forgiven.
We have become experts at wanting what God gives while quietly negotiating away what God asks.
And maybe that is why this strange passage reaches farther into the heart than we expected.
Because underneath the question, “Why could one brother marry another brother's widow?” lies another question:
What does covenant love do when obedience becomes costly?
It doesn't simply ask, “What can I get?”
It asks, “What faithfulness is required of me?”
There is another beautiful detail people sometimes miss.

Deuteronomy did not portray the brother as a mindless breeding instrument with absolutely no possibility of refusal. The verses immediately following describe what happened if he refused: the widow could go before the elders, and the public ceremony known later as chalitzah followed. His refusal carried shame because he would not “build up his brother's house,” but the text itself acknowledges the possibility of refusal.
So this wasn't Leviticus accidentally saying one thing and Deuteronomy accidentally saying another.

Later Jewish legal discussion wrestled explicitly with the relationship between the prohibition concerning a brother's wife and the exceptional command of levirate marriage. That very tension became a serious subject of interpretation rather than something ancient readers simply failed to notice.
And centuries later...
Jesus walked directly into this conversation.
The Sadducees came to Him with a scenario about seven brothers.
One brother dies childless.
His brother marries the widow.
Then that brother dies.
Then another.
And another.
Until their deliberately extreme scenario has the same woman married successively to seven brothers.
They were drawing upon the very law we have been discussing.
They asked Jesus whose wife she would be in the resurrection.
But they weren't sincerely trying to understand marriage.
They were attempting to make resurrection look absurd.
And Jesus refused to be trapped inside their assumptions.
“You are wrong,” He told them, because they did not understand the Scriptures or the power of God.
Then He explained that resurrection life cannot simply be reduced to an endless extension of present earthly marriage structures.
Think about that.
The law created to deal with the tragedy of death eventually became part of a debate in which Jesus proclaimed that death itself does not have the final word.
The Sadducees brought Jesus a puzzle about dead husbands.
Jesus answered them with the living God.
“He is not God of the dead, but of the living.”
And there...
right there...
the ancient law begins pointing our eyes toward something much greater than itself.
We should be careful here.
Deuteronomy 25 is not secretly a direct prophecy saying, “This is Jesus.” We should never force Christ into a passage by pretending its historical meaning does not matter.
Its immediate concern is Israelite family responsibility after a childless man's death.

But within the larger biblical story, themes of family redemption, preserving a name, protecting the vulnerable, costly faithfulness, and life confronting death belong to a trajectory that finds its ultimate hope in Christ.
Because humanity has a problem infinitely greater than a disappearing family name.
We have sin.
We have guilt.
We have death.
And no human relative can finally rescue us from the grave.
Then Jesus comes.
Not exploiting our helplessness.
Entering it.
Not owing us anything.
Giving Himself anyway.
Not preserving merely an earthly family name.
Bringing sinners into the family of God.
Not simply postponing death.
Defeating it.
The Gospel says that the eternal Son took on flesh, entered our broken human condition, bore sin at the cross, died, was buried, and rose again.
Our deepest scandal met God's astonishing grace.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years believing your scandal has already written the final chapter.
The affair.
The addiction.
The secret messages.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The abortion you still cry about.
The marriage you helped destroy.
The bitterness you keep feeding.
The church wound you used as permission to walk away from God.
The double life.
The years of pretending.
The night you wish you could erase.
The prayers you stopped praying because you became convinced God was tired of hearing your voice.
Maybe people know your worst chapter.
Maybe nobody does.
But Jesus does.
And He walked toward the cross knowing exactly what kind of sinners He was dying to save.
That does not make sin small.
The cross proves sin is more serious than our culture wants to admit.
But the same cross proves grace is more powerful than our shame wants us to believe.
Repentance is not pretending your scandal never happened.
Repentance is finally bringing your rebellion into the light, turning from it, and running toward the Christ whose blood is sufficient for sinners.
Grace is not God calling evil good.
Grace is God rescuing guilty people who could never make themselves righteous.
You do not need a prettier past.
You need a Savior.
You do not need to rewrite your history until you look innocent.
You need Jesus to redeem the sinner standing inside that history.
Maybe this article started as a Bible question for you.
“How can Leviticus forbid what Deuteronomy commands?”
Interesting question.
But Scripture has a habit of turning the question around.
What if the deeper contradiction isn't sitting in the Bible?
What if it is sitting inside us?
We call Jesus Lord...
but keep certain rooms locked.
We sing about surrender...
while negotiating obedience.
We ask God for mercy...
while refusing to forgive.
We want Him to expose biblical contradictions...
while praying He never exposes ours.
And still Christ calls.
Come out of hiding.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Me.
No performance.
No religious costume.
No carefully edited Christian profile.
Just truth meeting grace at the feet of Jesus.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't write an essay defending yourself.
Maybe your first act of honesty can be painfully simple.
Sometimes a comment is not merely engagement.
Sometimes it is the moment somebody finally stops hiding.
One share may put this in front of the person who has been silently questioning Scripture.
One share may reach the believer who thought difficult questions meant weak faith.
One share may find someone awake at 2:00 a.m., carrying a scandal they believe Jesus could never forgive.
There will come a day when someone asks you about this supposed contradiction, and you may want the Hebrew and context in front of you rather than trying to remember a thirty-second explanation.
It doesn't.
Only Christ saves.
And not because supporting Gospel Warrior can replace the biblical responsibilities God has placed upon you toward your local church, your family, the poor, or other Gospel work.
But voluntary generosity can help Gospel ministry continue.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should not be extracted through spiritual pressure: “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And if you cannot financially support the ministry, do not believe for one second that you are less valuable here.
Pray.
Save biblical teaching.
The mission was never to create customers.
It is to point people toward Jesus.
Because eventually every one of us becomes the person standing helpless before something we cannot undo.
A death we cannot reverse.
A wound we cannot erase.
A sin we cannot make innocent.
A past we cannot rewrite.
And that is precisely where the Gospel becomes more than religious vocabulary.
We couldn't rewrite ourselves.
So Jesus entered the story.
The cross tells the truth about our scandal.
The empty tomb announces that the scandal doesn't have to get the final sentence.
And perhaps that is the line you need to carry with you tonight:
Your darkest chapter may explain how you arrived here—but when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ, it does not get to decide how your story ends.
